as_told: At an open-air rave in Russia, the laser show was pointed straight into the crowd instead of at the sky. The beams blinded the audience, and many people were left with permanent eye damage.
lesson: Powerful laser beams aimed into a crowd can seriously damage people's eyes.
what_happened: At the Aquamarine open-air techno festival in the Vladimir region of Russia on 5 July 2008, a laser was aimed at the audience. NTV reported on 14 July 2008 that the festival ended in urgent hospital treatment for dozens of people, with a preliminary diagnosis of haemorrhage on the fundus and retina; the victims themselves said there were at least 60 of them in Moscow. On 15 July Kommersant reported that roughly 30 people went to Moscow clinics, that doctors found haemorrhagic retinopathy rather than retinal burns, and that the number of patients reached 12. The injured people lost part of their sight; one could not read 20-centimetre letters with his right eye. No report I found says that the audience as a whole was blinded.
false_part: The audience was not blinded: between 12 and about 60 people (the counts differ by source) had retinal haemorrhages and partial loss of sight.

lesson_verdict.why: A multi-centre case series from Kolhapur, India, found retinal injury (premacular haemorrhage) in 51 people after recreational laser shows. Most eyes recovered good vision after treatment, but complications were not uncommon, so the danger is real even though permanent blindness was rare.

source.what: Joglekar et al., 'A retrospective analysis of presentation and outcomes in a cluster outbreak of non-occupational laser exposure retinopathy', Journal Français d'Ophtalmologie 48(4):104470, 2025 (abstract)
source.quote: The study included a total of 51 eyes of 51 patients, all of whom reported exposure to recreational laser shows.

search_steps: The web search tool had no budget left when I started, so I used only direct addresses and catalogue searches (Wikipedia, PubMed, archive.org).
Wikipedia 'Laser lighting display' and 'Laser safety': no mention of the event. Wikipedia 'Audience scanning' links an ILDA statement on the 'July 5, 2008 Russian accident'.

laserist.org page now returns 404; saved the December 2008 Wayback copy. ILDA (a laser-show industry body) names the Aquamarine Open Air Festival near Moscow and says news reports began on 14 July; it is commentary on press reports, so I used it only as a lead.

Followed ILDA's two news links: saved the Wayback copies of NTV (14 July 2008, Russian) and Kommersant English edition (15 July 2008). NTV page is cp1251; I quote from the UTF-8 text file made from it.
PubMed search for laser show retinal injury found one case series (Joglekar et al. 2025); saved the abstract. I found no published medical follow-up of the Aquamarine patients.
confidence_note: The festival date, 5 July 2008, comes only from the ILDA page, which I treat as a lead; NTV and Kommersant say only that it happened about a week before their reports. The counts conflict: NTV says dozens were hospitalised and victims claim at least 60; Kommersant says about 30 sought care and 12 were patients. Kommersant also quotes an anonymous medical source who suggested drug use might be the real cause; ILDA, judging from video, thought pulsed lasers were the cause. I found no record of the long-term outcome. The lesson source is an abstract only, and it studies Indian laser shows, not this event.
